# Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays (Lovitt, 1977)

## Bibliographic identity

The selected English carrier is Martin Heidegger, *The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays*, translated and introduced by William Lovitt (New York: Harper & Row, 1977). This single recoverable volume houses the two essays the essay consumes: the title essay, "The Question Concerning Technology" (pp. 3–35; German "Die Frage nach der Technik," 1954, from *Vorträge und Aufsätze*), and "The Age of the World Picture" (pp. 115–154; German "Die Zeit des Weltbildes," 1938, from *Holzwege*). All locators in this house are keyed to the 1977 Harper & Row pagination.

### Edition trap: Lovitt 1977 vs. Krell's revised text

Widely circulated PDFs of "The Question Concerning Technology" silently carry David Farrell Krell's revised text from *Basic Writings*, not Lovitt's 1977 rendering, while presenting themselves as the 1977 volume. Known divergences caught this cycle: Lovitt "to reveal the real" vs. Krell "to reveal the actual"; Lovitt "conceive and push forward the technological" vs. Krell "represent and pursue the technological"; Lovitt "courses through them in their folded togetherness" vs. Krell "pervades them in their folded contiguity." The house pins Lovitt 1977 as the canonical wording; any quotation promoted from this house must be checked against that printing, not against a *Basic Writings*-derived file.

## Source scholarship

The title essay stakes everything on a distinction announced at the outset: "the essence of technology is by no means anything technological" (p. 4). Heidegger's route to that essence runs backward through the Greek vocabulary of production. Against the instrumental-anthropological definition of technology (correct but not true), he argues that "Technology is a way of revealing" (p. 12) — a mode of alētheuein, of bringing beings out of concealment. Technē belongs with epistēmē — "Both words are names for knowing in the widest sense" (p. 13) — and "It is as revealing, and not as manufacturing, that technē is a bringing-forth" (p. 13): technē belongs to poiēsis, and the essay's warrant for poiēsis is Plato's Symposium 205b, rendered by Lovitt as "Every occasion for whatever passes over and goes forward into presencing from that which is not presencing is poiesis, is bringing-forth [Her-vor-bringen]" (p. 10). What distinguishes modern technology from the windmill and the silver chalice is not machinery but the mode of revealing that rules it: "a challenging [Herausfordern], which puts to nature the unreasonable demand that it supply energy that can be extracted and stored as such" (p. 14). The Rhine example carries the diagnosis concretely — the hydroelectric plant "sets the Rhine to supplying its hydraulic pressure" (p. 16), the river "dammed up into the power works," against "'The Rhine' as uttered out of the art work, in Hölderlin's hymn by that name."

What challenging-forth produces is not objects but Bestand: "Everywhere everything is ordered to stand by, to be immediately at hand, indeed to stand there just so that it may be on call for a further ordering. Whatever is ordered about in this way has its own standing. We call it the standing-reserve [Bestand]" (p. 17). The naming of Ge-stell is prepared by a philological move on the German collective prefix Ge- as gathering: "That which primordially unfolds the mountains into mountain ranges and courses through them in their folded togetherness is the gathering that we call 'Gebirg' [mountain chain]. That original gathering from which unfold the ways in which we have feelings of one kind or another we name 'Gemüt' [disposition]. We now name that challenging claim which gathers man thither to order the self-revealing as standing-reserve: 'Ge-stell' [Enframing]" (p. 19). The formal definition follows: "Enframing means the gathering together of that setting-upon which sets upon man, i.e., challenges him forth, to reveal the real, in the mode of ordering, as standing-reserve," and "Enframing means that way of revealing which holds sway in the essence of modern technology and which is itself nothing technological" (p. 20). Enframing, decisively, is itself a gathering — a gathering that arrests everything gathered into orderability.

The essay's late movement turns the danger inward: man himself "comes to the point where he himself will have to be taken as standing-reserve" (pp. 26–27), and yet "precisely as the one so threatened, exalts himself to the posture of lord of the earth" (p. 27). Heidegger frames Heisenberg's observation — "It seems as though man everywhere and always encounters only himself" (p. 27) — only to invert it: "In truth, however, precisely nowhere does man today any longer encounter himself, i.e., his essence" (p. 27). The essay closes on Hölderlin's "But where danger is, grows / The saving power also" (p. 28, requoted p. 34) and on its last line, "For questioning is the piety of thought" (p. 35).

"The Age of the World Picture" gives the historical register of the same diagnosis. The modern age is not one in which humanity acquires a picture of the world among other possible pictures; rather, "world picture, when understood essentially, does not mean a picture of the world but the world conceived and grasped as picture" (p. 129, page flagged for print check). This is not a representational accident but the fundamental event of the epoch: "The fundamental event of the modern age is the conquest of the world as picture" (p. 134, independently corroborated). The event has a subjective face: "that the world becomes picture is one and the same event with the event of man's becoming subiectum in the midst of that which is" (p. 132) — "Man becomes the relational center of that which is as such" (p. 128, flagged). The mechanism is Vorstellen: "To represent [vor-stellen] means to bring what is present at hand [das Vorhandene] before oneself as something standing over against, to relate it to oneself, to the one representing it, and to force it back into this relationship to oneself as the normative realm" (p. 131, flagged ±1). World-as-picture and man-as-subiectum are two names for one seizure.

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

Heidegger supplies the essay's canonical articulation of the calculative/enframing pole: revealing as challenging-forth, the world converted to standing-reserve, Ge-stell as a gathering, and the world-picture diagnosis of representational seizure. The Ge-/gathering passage (q008) is the load-bearing textual site for the essay's counterfeit-gathering reading.

### Licensed essay use

- Establish enframing as a mode of revealing that gathers — the textual basis against which the essay develops its own distinction between gatherings.
- Carry the world-picture diagnosis into the essay's world-picture-to-world-atlas argument.
- Supply the standing-reserve and man-as-standing-reserve material for the preference and attunement sections.
- Hold the Symposium 205b citation as the essay's bridge point into the Platonic banquet (see q004 use-notes).

### Claim boundary

Heidegger does not supply the essay's counterfeit-gathering reading — that is the essay's Argued development of the Ge-/gathering passage, not a claim found in Heidegger or the secondary literature. No scholarship connects QCT to Odyssey 8; the Homeric net mapping is the essay's own move. The constructive return is likewise the essay's: it explicitly departs from Heidegger's fatalism. The venue context (Bratton's hostility to Heideggerian mood) is recorded in the workshop's venue notes, not here.
